list.listitem: Chronic diarrhea is defined as increased stool frequency of more than 3 per day, stool weight greater than 200 g per day, decreased fecal consistency, and all this occurring for over 4 weeks. C

Classify diarrhea into three categories with the aid of the history, physical examination, and preliminary testing: (1) watery (osmotic or secretory), (2) bloody or pus (inflammatory), or (3) fatty. C
Initial tests include measurement of fecal osmolality for watery diarrhea, presence or absence of fecal leukocytes for inflammatory diarrhea, and measurement of stool fat for fatty diarrhea. C
Specific therapy depends on the underlying cause. C

background.definition: Chronic diarrhea is defined as increased stool frequency (more than 3 per day), increased stool weight (greater than 200 g per day), decreased stool consistency, and lasting at least 4 weeks. British guidelines on chronic diarrhea in adults defines chronic diarrhea as "the persistent alteration from the norm with stool consistency between types 5 and 7 on Bristol stool chart and increased frequency greater than 4 weeks duration," where Bristol 5 is soft blobs with clear-cut edges passed easily and Bristol 7 is entirely liquid.

list.listitem: The prevalence is approximately 5%; numbers vary depending on definition, study design, and sample population.
$661 million per year in both direct and indirect cost of chronic diarrhea.
See .

Secretory diarrhea is caused by an abnormality in the intestinal electrolyte transport system (that persists despite fasting) or a stimulus such as a toxin, peptide, or derivative of arachidonic acids that impairs the transport system.
Osmotic diarrhea is caused by an osmotic agent that draws fluid into the lumen and usually resolves with fasting or discontinuation of the offending agent.
Inflammatory diarrhea results from intestinal mucosal damage causing blood and pus in stools.

Fatty diarrhea is caused by malabsorption or maldigestion. Malabsorption is associated with small intestinal mucosal disease. In maldigestion, absorption is intact but digestion is impaired because of pancreatic insufficiency or biliary abnormalities.

Allergic reactions to foods, ie, non-IgE-mediated gastrointestinal food-induced allergic disorders (most commonly from cow's milk, soy, rice and oats), are associated with non-bloody diarrhea, malabsorption and failure to thrive among children up to 2 years of age.

Chronic diarrhea may be caused by one or more of the following mechanisms: Increased osmotic load in the gut lumen from a nonabsorbable substance. Decreased absorption from disruption of mucosal integrity. Increased electrolyte secretion from disruption of intestinal electrolyte transport system. Abnormal intestinal motility with increase transit through the lumen, limiting absorption time.
It is important to correlate diagnostic testing with the information elicited from the history and physical. C
Separate diarrhea into three categories for directed testing: watery (osmotic or secretory), bloody or pus (inflammatory), or fatty. C

Initial tests include measurement of osmotic gap for watery diarrhea, presence of absence of fecal leukocytes or fecal calprotectin for inflammatory diarrhea, and measurement of stool fat for fatty diarrhea. C

list.listitem: Because a variety of disorders are associated with chronic diarrhea, a comprehensive history is essential in directing further testing. Physical examination alone rarely provides a specific diagnosis but mainly helps to narrow possibilities. The initial step is to characterize the diarrhea by type of stool (watery, bloody, fatty) and note onset, pattern, duration, and any incontinence.
Ask the patient about recent travel and consumption of possibly contaminated food or water (including untreated well water, or river or lake water).
Associated abdominal pain suggests inflammatory bowel disease, irritable bowel syndrome, or ischemia.
Associated weight loss suggests nutrient malabsorption, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, or neoplasm.
Aggravating or improving factors aid in identifying potential causes from diet or stress (eg, inflammatory bowel disease).

If there are past medical/surgical/psychiatric history such as drugs, chemotherapy, radiation, gastrointestinal surgery, eating disorders, or malingering, consider systemic diseases as hyperthyroidism, diabetes, collagen vascular diseases, or immunodeficiency.

Pertinent findings on physical examination include oral ulcers (Crohn’s disease), thyroid mass (hyperthyroidism), heart murmur or wheezing (carcinoid), hepatosplenomegaly, mass, ascites, tenderness (liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease), skin flushing, rash, edema (Crohn’s disease), perianal fistula, abscess, and sphincter tone (fecal incontinence).
Frankly bloody diarrhea strongly suggests invasive disease. Tenesmus and moderate or heavy mucus suggests invasive disease in patients with nonbloody diarrhea.

The following stool studies should be initially obtained: fecal pH (<6.0 suggests carbohydrate malabsorption in patients with high osmotic gap watery diarrhea); fecal fats (quantitative and microscopy) ; fecal leukocytes; fecal calpoprotein fecal lactoferrin for ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease;, fecal electrolytes and osmolality; and fecal blood.

If possible, a quantitative 48-hour to 72-hour collection may be helpful to further assess stool weight or steatorrhea. Depending on preliminary findings, specific testing may be used to narrow the diagnosis (see ).
If the stool contains white blood cells, obtain a fecal culture.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is now used to detect parasitic DNA and some bacterial pathogens (eg, campylobacter, salmonella, yersinia) in stool samples, when suspected.

Colonoscopy with biopsy may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis. Among 23 patients with persistent diarrhea following renal transplant, ileocolonoscopy identified mucosal abnormalities in 19, including 11 cases of infection (36.6%) and 10 drug-related cases (33.3%).

British Society of Gastroenterology recommendations for the evaluation of adults with chronic diarrhea include the following: (1) Oerform a detailed history and physical, and order a complete blood count (followed by ferritin if anemic), a thyroid-stimulating hormone test, and serology for celiac disease (tissue transglutaminase or antiendomysium). (2) Test stool for Clostridium difficile, ova and parasites, and calprotectin (abnormal inflammatory bowel disease), and consider a fecal immunochemical test. (3) In patients with altered bowel habits, rule out colorectal cancer with colonoscopy. In patients without frank rectal bleeding, order fecal immunochemical testing to exclude cancer. (4) If symptoms persist, refer for further investigation. (5) Further testing could include hydrogen breath test for lactose intolerance, video capsule endoscopy, fecal elastase testing for fat malabsorption, tests for bile acid diarrhea, and magnetic resonance imaging for the evaluation of chronic pancreatitis.

The American Gastroenterological Association guideline (2019) suggests the following tests for patients with chronic diarrhea (ie, watery diarrhea for at least 4 weeks): fecal calprotectin or fecal lactoferrin to screen for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and testing for giardiasis, celiac disease, and bile acid diarrhea. They recommend not screening for ova and parasites unless the patient has come from a high-risk area. They also recommend against using erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) to screen for IBD.

When there is a high probability that a proposed diagnosis is correct (eg, a carcinoid tumor accompanied by classic findings such as flushing, heart murmur, and an enlarged liver), specific testing for that diagnosis is appropriate.

shows a suggested approach when there is no clear or obvious diagnosis, based on the classification of diarrhea as watery, inflammatory, or fatty. The second, more widely used strategy, consists of categorizing, testing, and treating. More specific testing is directed by preliminary findings (see ).

For functional or self-limiting conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, the patient may be empirically treated after life-threatening conditions are ruled out. Additional tests are deferred awaiting response to initial treatment.

Three different strategies can be applied to the management of chronic diarrhea: (1) test and treat; (2) categorize, test, and treat; and (3) empiric therapy. C
Test and treat: It assumes that the proposed diagnosis probability is high given a particular presentation. C Categorize, test, and treat: Preliminary testing helps narrow down possibilities after the history and physical examination findings are nonspecific. C Empiric therapy: This strategy is applicable if life-threatening and specific treatment conditions can be excluded from the presentation; remaining conditions are usually self limiting. C

Drug treatment for chronic diarrhea is targeted at correcting the underlying abnormal intestinal motility. When no underlying cause is evident, a trial of symptomatic agents can be used to alter abnormal intestinal motility.

For bile acids malabsorption and antibiotic-induced colitis use bile sequestrants, such as cholestyramine (Questran) 4 g 2 to 4 times a day, that act as an anion exchange resin that possesses strong acidic binding properties.

Give antibiotics in cases of small bowel bacterial overgrowth or other infectious agents such as Clostridium difficile (pseudomembranous colitis), shigellosis, giardiasis, or entamoeba histolytica. In a study of 20 patients with myotonic muscular dystrophy type 1, thirteen (65%) had small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, detected by a positive glucose breath hydrogen test. Diarrhea was the most common complaint and 70% of patients had a good response to antibiotics, most commonly ciprofloxacin.
Probiotics decrease the risk of antibiotic-associated diarrhea by 50% (NNT = 8).

In children aged 0 to 18 years the probiotics Lactobacilli rhamnosus or Saccharomyces boulardii (5-40 million colony forming units/day) prevented antibiotic-associated diarrhea (NNT = 10). Evidence for the efficacy and safety of other probiotic agents for pediatric AAD is lacking.

Carcinoid and neuroendocrine tumors: somatostatin analogues, such as octreotide with its antisecretory effect, decrease hormone secretion of the tumor and decrease motility. Clonidine, an alpha-adrenergic agonist, acts through the inhibition of motility, and is useful in carcinoid as well as short-bowel syndromes.
For inflammatory bowel disease, see chapters on Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis.

Symptomatic therapy with natural or synthetic opiates reduces the number of bowel movements and improves stool consistency by increasing intestinal circular smooth muscle tone and decreasing intestinal secretion. Diphenoxylate with atropine (Lomotil 5 mg, 4 times a day) or loperamide (Imodium 4 mg, then 2 mg as needed up to a maximum of 16 mg/day), are effective, rapid acting, and long lasting. Natural opiates such as morphine or codeine have limited use because of abuse potential, central sedation, and nausea.

For symptomatic treatment, stool bulking agents such as psyllium, methylcellulose, polycarbophil, and silicates (kaolin) can aid with binding bacterial toxins. Bismuth subsalicylate, an anti-inflammatory with specific prostaglandin inhibition, causes decreased fluid production mainly helpful in acute diarrhea caused by microorganisms and enterotoxins.
Proton pump inhibitors are helpful in blocking gastric acid secretion that may lead to diarrhea in patients with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
For systemic mastocytosis, histamine receptor blockers inhibit mast cell production and hypersecretion.
Indomethacin, a prostaglandin inhibitor, can aid in treatment from diarrhea caused by medullary thyroid cancer.

Among 120 patients with urgency and episodic incontinence associated with irritable bowel syndrome, ondansetron was associated with less fecal urgency, decreased frequency of defecation and less bloating, but no change in pain scores compared to placebo.

Eluxadoline (a mixed mu and kappa opoid agonist—similar to loperamide—and a delta opiod receptor antagonist) relieves IBS by decreasing visceral hypersensitivity. In a report of 2427 patients with IBS, the NNT for the outcome of decreased abdominal pain and improvement in stool consistency of at least 50%, was 9 to 14 compared to placebo.The active treatment group experienced more adverse effects (pancreatitis, spasm of the sphincter of Oddi and cardiovascular events).

In children living in areas where the prevalance of malnutrition or zinc deficiency is high (ie, Asian countries) who have acute or persistent diarrhea, oral zinc supplementation may be beneficial in children older than 6 months.

Enterosgel (polymethylsiloxane polyhydrate) is an intestinal absorbent that is not pharmacologically active and is approved for over-the-counter purchase. Among 440 patients randomized to receive enterosgel or matching placebo, significantly more patients in the enterosgel group reported a 30% or greater decrease in abdominal pain and at least a 50% reduction in diarrheal stools at 8 weeks (37.4% vs 24.3%; P = .002; NNT = 8). Adverse effects did not differ between the 2 groups.
Surgical resection or management of complications such as fistula formation in Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis.
Possible surgical resection of tumors when appropriate.

A trial of limiting common dietary causes (eg, sugar substitutes, milk products, caffeine, sugary foods and fruits, and alcohol) might be appropriate. This can help to avoid early unnecessary testing.

Consider a trial of a lactose-free or a fructose-free diet. However, with respect to lactose intolerance, most studies found that approximately 1 cup of milk could be taken as a single dose with no symptoms or minor symptoms and more when taken with other foods. Lactose-reduced milk did not consistently reduce gastrointestinal symptoms and the limited data on lactase supplementation was conflicting. Probiotics were no more effective than regular milk in patients with pre-existing symptoms.
Avoid sugar substitutes or other ingredients that may contain nonabsorbable compounds such as sorbitol.

In one study of children in rural Bangladesh, cooked green bananas added to the diet increased cure rates in prolonged diarrhea (HR prolonged = 0.38; 95% CI, 0.26-0.59) and resulted in higher recovery rates by day 10 (79.8% vs 51.9%) and day 14 (93.6% vs 67.2%).

Consider hospitalization if the patient experiences dehydration with difficulty maintaining hydration status, hemodynamic instability, significant electrolyte abnormality, symptomatic hypotension, or severe anemia.
Volume replacement should be the first step in the management of diarrhea by either oral rehydration or intravenous fluid replacement with either Ringer’s lactate solution or saline solution.
Give electrolyte replacement and blood transfusion, as indicated.
The prognosis is variable depending on whether the specific cause can be easily cured. C
Teach the patients the signs and symptoms of dehydration. C

History and physical; order initial stool studies for stool osmolality, pH, blood, WBC, fat; categorize type of diarrhea.
Secretory diarrhea (see ). Consider stool culture, specific endocrine testing, drug induced, GI structural imaging.
Carbohydrate malabsorption; consider hydrogen breath test.
Osmotic laxative use; check magnesium, phosphate, or sulfate.
Consider cancer, inflammatory bowel disease; evaluate with imaging/endoscopy.
Low fat (<9.5 g/100 g) or high fat (≥9.5/100 g)?

feature.caption: Causes of Chronic Diarrhea by Type.

tr.td: ● Chronic bacterial infections (eg, G. lamblia, E. histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Aeromonas, Plesiomonas, E. coli, C. difficile, M. tuberculosis, Y. enterocolitica, V. cholerae)
● Endocrine disorders (eg, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, Addison disease, autonomic neuropathy)
● Motility disorders (eg, irritable bowel syndrome, surgical [eg, vagotomy])

● Drug related (antibiotics, beta blockers, digitalis, quinidine, chemotherapy, NSAIDs, colchicine, laxatives, ricinoleic acid, phenolphthalein, anthraquinone, diuretics, theophylline, cholinergic agents, prostaglandins)
● Neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma, vasoactive intestinal, somatostatinoma, mastocytosis, carcinoid syndrome, medullary thyroid carcinoma, Zollinger-Ellison tumor, villous adenoma, lymphoma)
● Carbohydrate malabsorption (eg, lactose, sorbitol, mannitol, fructose)
● Parasitic infection (eg, amebiasis, strongyloides, Cryptosporidium parvum)
